headline: High risk: shared file and network surfaces make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests PDFs, text, images, and draw.io content and uses MCP/browser/network paths; Agent B reads and writes filesystem artifacts and runs an interactive CLI. If B consumes A-produced files or diagrams, attacker-controlled content can steer downstream instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred from both profiles.
conditions: IF Agent B parses files generated by Agent A as instructions or commands
IF a shared workspace or mounted directory is used between the agents
mitigations: Disable automatic execution of content from A in B
Use separate directories with read-only handoff files
Strip active content from PDFs/diagrams before handoff
Add a manual review step before B processes A outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A handles API keys and broad network egress; Agent B touches certificate private keys, registry credentials, and environment variables while also having broad egress. If they share a workspace or credentials path, sensitive material can flow from one agent to the other and out over the network. The pairwise leakage path is plausible from both profiles.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same filesystem or environment variables
IF either agent forwards its context or file contents to external APIs
mitigations: Separate secrets into per-agent vaults
Mount distinct workspaces with no shared write access
Redact keys and certificates before any transfer
Block outbound network except allowlisted endpoints
Rotate any credentials exposed to either agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can use MCP and broad network egress, while Agent B can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. If they operate on the same directory, concurrent writes or conflicting side effects can corrupt outputs or overwrite artifacts. No locking or shared-state protection is documented, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or artifact set
IF the orchestrator does not provide file locking or transaction boundaries
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Make one agent read-only
Snapshot inputs before each run
Use a staging directory for merges

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A produces AI-assisted visualizations from documents, and Agent B is an interactive CLI that can act on filesystem artifacts. If B treats A's generated diagrams or text as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect container or filesystem actions. The pathway exists, but B is not documented as fully autonomous, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF B consumes A outputs without verification
IF A-generated artifacts are used as the sole source for B commands or edits
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against source files
Add checksum or diff checks before acting
Keep A outputs advisory, not authoritative
Insert a human approval step for destructive actions

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles API keys and documents; Agent B handles certificate private keys, registry credentials, and environment variables. If regulated or sensitive data is routed through both, retention and residency obligations can diverge, especially because both use broad network egress and third-party APIs. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed by both agents under different retention policies
IF either agent sends sensitive data to a third-party service without a DPA
mitigations: Document data classes allowed for each agent
Align retention and deletion settings
Route regulated data only through approved systems
Review vendor DPAs and residency settings
Exclude private keys and credentials from both workflows
